question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q07
question.questiontext: A script draft has stage directions mixed into spoken dialogue. What revision best supports the reader?

answer.answertext: Remove all stage directions from the play.
Add a title but leave the dialogue confusing.
Replace all character names with initials without explanation.
Format stage directions consistently so they do not look like spoken lines.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q08
question.questiontext: Which publication note is strongest?

answer.answertext: I submitted it because I was finished.
I used stanza breaks to separate the three image groups so the reader can follow the poem's movement.
I changed things randomly until it looked different.
I used a bright font because readers like color.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q09
question.questiontext: What is the purpose of previewing a file before submission?

answer.answertext: To avoid reading the piece again.
To add more draft comments.
To see the piece the way a reader will see it.
To change the genre at the last minute.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q10
question.questiontext: Which choice best describes format-specific quality work?

answer.answertext: Every genre uses exactly the same format.
The writer adds as many visual effects as possible.
The file name is left blank.
The piece is formatted so its genre is clear and readable.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q11
question.questiontext: A student includes a note at the top that says "rough version, maybe final." What should happen before submission?

answer.answertext: Remove the draft label and submit a clearly final version.
Leave it because it is honest.
Add more uncertain notes.
Hide the title instead.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q12
question.questiontext: Which conventions pass is most appropriate for a final publication version?

answer.answertext: Rewrite the entire piece into a new topic.
Ignore dialogue punctuation because it is creative writing.
Check capitalization, punctuation, spelling, and paragraphing without changing intentional style.
Add misspellings to make the piece unique.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q13
question.questiontext: Which answer best explains why a title matters in digital publication?

answer.answertext: A title replaces the need for formatting.
A title can prepare the reader and make the piece look complete.
A title should always reveal the ending.
A title is only needed for research papers.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q14
question.questiontext: A writer uses different spacing styles for each character label in a script. What problem does this create?

answer.answertext: It makes the script too poetic.
It automatically improves performance.
It removes the need for stage directions.
It can confuse readers about who is speaking and how the scene is organized.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q15
question.questiontext: Which action best prepares a portfolio piece for online collaborative publication?

answer.answertext: Check that the final version is clear, complete, readable, and named correctly.
Submit a version with unresolved comments.
Use unclear labels so readers ask questions.
Remove all formatting from every genre.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q16
question.questiontext: Why should a writer remove placeholder labels such as "fix this later"?

answer.answertext: They prove the writer revised carefully.
They are required in every final draft.
They make the piece look unfinished and distract the reader.
They replace the need for a publication note.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q17
question.questiontext: Which sentence best distinguishes formatting from decoration?

answer.answertext: Formatting means adding unrelated pictures.
Formatting supports readability and genre; decoration may be visual but not always useful.
Decoration always improves publication quality.
Formatting is only about making text smaller.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q18
question.questiontext: Which example shows a reader-ready opening?

answer.answertext: No title, no author label, and a draft note.
Random blank lines before the first sentence.
A warning that the writer did not proofread.
A clear title, clean first paragraph, and no leftover drafting comments.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q19
question.questiontext: A student says, "I cannot change any spacing because the words are already revised." What is the best response?

answer.answertext: Spacing is part of publication readiness and can be revised without changing meaning.
Spacing never matters.
Only teachers can decide line breaks.
Publication formatting means rewriting the whole piece.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q20
question.questiontext: Which final check best supports clarity, cohesion, and conventions?

answer.answertext: Only check the last word.
Trust that spellcheck catches everything.
Read one sentence, line, or script beat at a time to catch distracting errors.
Add longer words to sound formal.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q21
question.questiontext: Which formatting choice best supports a poem's pacing?

answer.answertext: Break every word into separate letters.
Remove all stanza breaks because poems should be crowded.
Use paragraph indentation for every line without purpose.
Put an important final phrase on its own line when the pause supports meaning.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q22
question.questiontext: What should a writer do if the digital preview shows broken spacing?

answer.answertext: Ignore it because the draft looked fine earlier.
Fix the spacing and preview again before submission.
Submit a screenshot instead of the assignment.
Add a note telling readers to imagine the spacing.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q23
question.questiontext: Which response best explains online collaborative publication?

answer.answertext: Writing is prepared so others can access, read, and respond to it in a shared digital space.
Writing is hidden so no one can read it.
Writing is submitted with no title and no format.
Writing is changed into a spreadsheet.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q24
question.questiontext: Which mistake would most likely lower publication quality?

answer.answertext: Using consistent paragraphing in a story.
Leaving unresolved comments, random spacing, and a missing title in the final file.
Previewing the file before submission.
Explaining a purposeful formatting choice.

question.name: CW_U06_L05_R_Q25
question.questiontext: Which final submission choice is best?

answer.answertext: Submit only a rough outline with no title.
Submit every draft without identifying the final version.
Submit the final formatted piece and a note explaining how format supports the reader.
Submit a file with draft comments still visible.

question_category.name: Default for U6L6 Q
question_category.info: The default category for questions shared in context 'U6L6 Q'.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q01
question.questiontext: What should an author presentation do before the excerpt is read?

answer.answertext: Avoid giving any context at all.
Explain every event in the full story.
Introduce the title, genre, brief context, and listening focus.
Apologize for the piece before reading.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q02
question.questiontext: Which statement best identifies presentation purpose?

answer.answertext: I want the audience to understand how my revised dialogue shows tension.
I want to talk until time runs out.
I want to avoid explaining the piece.
I want the audience to guess everything.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q03
question.questiontext: A student chooses a long chapter that requires ten minutes of plot explanation. What is the best revision to the plan?

answer.answertext: Keep the whole chapter because longer is always stronger.
Select a shorter excerpt that shows the key craft choice with brief context.
Remove all context and hope the audience follows.
Replace the presentation with a written quiz.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q04
question.questiontext: Which choice is plot summary instead of craft reasoning?

answer.answertext: I used repeated s sounds to slow the poem's ending.
I revised dialogue so the reader can infer discomfort.
I placed the final image alone so the audience pauses.
The character leaves home, meets a friend, and returns later.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q05
question.questiontext: Which speaking note style best supports a presentation?

answer.answertext: Short key phrases in the planned sequence.
A full essay copied word for word in tiny font.
No notes at all even if the sequence is complex.
Random words with no connection to the excerpt.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q06
question.questiontext: Why should the presenter name a listening focus?

answer.answertext: It replaces the need to read the excerpt.
It allows the presenter to skip craft reasoning.
It tells the audience what craft choice to notice during the excerpt.
It hides the purpose from the audience.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q07
question.questiontext: Which is the strongest craft explanation?

answer.answertext: I wrote a poem because poems are short.
I placed the final line by itself so the reader pauses before the speaker's decision.
I like the ending most.
My story has an ending.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q08
question.questiontext: Which revision reflection is strongest?

answer.answertext: I fixed stuff.
I changed nothing and learned nothing.
I made it better somehow.
I revised the opening image to establish setting before conflict, which makes the scene easier to enter.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q09
question.questiontext: Which sequence best matches the lesson presentation structure?

answer.answertext: Title and genre, context, listening focus, excerpt, craft reasoning, revision reflection.
Excerpt, unrelated story, apology, ending.
Full plot summary, full draft history, no excerpt.
Title only, then stop.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q10
question.questiontext: A presenter says, "This is a poem about rain." What should be added to improve the plan?

answer.answertext: A longer unrelated biography.
A craft focus, such as image, sound, line break, or tone.
A statement that no one needs context.
A promise that the poem has no choices.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q11
question.questiontext: Which excerpt is easiest for an audience to understand?

answer.answertext: A section that starts mid-conflict with no names, no context, and unclear speakers.
The entire portfolio read without pause.
A focused section introduced with a brief explanation of situation and speaker.
A section the presenter cannot explain.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q12
question.questiontext: Which statement best communicates author growth?

answer.answertext: My first draft explained the fear directly; my revision used action so readers could infer it.
I wrote it the night before.
I did not revise anything.
The assignment was difficult.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q13
question.questiontext: What is the role of audience frame?

answer.answertext: It hides the title from the audience.
It replaces the excerpt.
It lists unrelated facts about the writer.
It gives readers or listeners the context they need before the excerpt.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q14
question.questiontext: A student's presentation notes include only "read poem, done." What is missing?

answer.answertext: More silence.
Title, context, listening focus, craft reasoning, and reflection.
Random decoration.
A hidden file name.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q15
question.questiontext: Which choice best explains why an excerpt should not require too much setup?

answer.answertext: Context is never allowed.
Long setup proves the piece is complex.
The audience should spend most of the presentation understanding the work and craft, not sorting through long background.
The presenter should avoid all explanation.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q16
question.questiontext: Which closing statement best fits an author presentation?

answer.answertext: This revision helped the final scene feel more tense because the reader now infers the conflict through dialogue.
That is all, and I do not know why I picked it.
I hope it was not confusing.
The story is over.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q17
question.questiontext: Which question should guide excerpt selection?

answer.answertext: Is this excerpt the longest possible?
Can I avoid talking about the excerpt?
Will this confuse the audience?
Does this excerpt show a craft choice I can explain clearly?

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q18
question.questiontext: Which presentation plan best avoids summary-only speaking?

answer.answertext: List every event in order and stop.
Name two craft choices and explain how each affects the reader.
Read the entire piece without any introduction.
Say the piece is good without evidence.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q19
question.questiontext: Which detail belongs in brief context before an excerpt?

answer.answertext: Every assignment the student completed all semester.
A list of favorite songs.
The speaker has just missed the last bus and is deciding whether to call home.
A full explanation of the ending before reading.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q20
question.questiontext: Which answer best describes communication of craft reasoning?

answer.answertext: Explaining how specific writing choices shape meaning or audience effect.
Saying the piece is finished.
Listing page numbers only.
Avoiding all terms from the lesson.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q21
question.questiontext: A presenter plans to discuss five unrelated craft choices in two minutes. What should the presenter do?

answer.answertext: Speak faster and keep all five.
Choose two or three focused points that connect to the purpose.
Remove the excerpt to make room.
Add more unrelated points.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q22
question.questiontext: Which phrase best signals a listening focus?

answer.answertext: Listen to everything and nothing.
I have no focus for this excerpt.
Ignore the language choices.
Listen for the repeated hard consonant sounds in the final stanza.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q23
question.questiontext: Which statement is too vague for mastery?

answer.answertext: I used dialogue to reveal tension between the characters.
I revised sentence length to change pacing.
I made it better.
I selected the excerpt because it shows the narrator's voice.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q24
question.questiontext: What should the presenter practice for timing and clarity?

answer.answertext: Only the final word.
A different assignment.
Avoiding the excerpt completely.
The sequence of title, context, excerpt, craft explanation, and reflection.

question.name: CW_U06_L06_R_Q25
question.questiontext: Which final plan best meets the lesson standard?

answer.answertext: A plan with title, genre, brief context, selected excerpt, listening focus, craft reasoning, and revision reflection.
A plan that only says the work is creative.
A plan with no excerpt and no craft explanation.
A plan that only summarizes the plot.

question_category.name: Default for U6L7 Q
question_category.info: The default category for questions shared in context 'U6L7 Q'.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_Q01
question.questiontext:
Question ID: CW_U06_L07_Q01

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.01

Which action best begins integrated portfolio preparation?

answer.answertext: List required parts and mark each present, missing, or needing revision.
answer.feedback: Correct. This answer is supported by MLA.CW.PUB.01 because it selects a specific craft move or revision decision: "List required parts and mark each present, missing, or needing revision.". That choice matches the prompt instead of giving a vague reaction, an unsupported preference, or a detail outside the draft. Use the same reasoning when you explain how a word, structure, voice, image, or revision choice affects the reader.

answer.answertext: Decorate the portfolio before checking contents.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. First check completeness and purpose. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: Submit the first file found.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Selection should be purposeful. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: Remove the author statement.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Reflection is part of portfolio synthesis. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_Q02
question.questiontext:
Question ID: CW_U06_L07_Q02

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.COM.01

Which piece belongs in a final portfolio?

answer.answertext: A piece with no title and no revision.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. This is not reader-ready. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: A favorite piece the writer cannot explain.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Preference alone is weak evidence. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: A revised piece that shows a specific craft skill and reader effect.
answer.feedback: Correct. This answer is supported by MLA.CW.COM.01 because it selects a specific craft move or revision decision: "A revised piece that shows a specific craft skill and reader effect.". That choice matches the prompt instead of giving a vague reaction, an unsupported preference, or a detail outside the draft. Use the same reasoning when you explain how a word, structure, voice, image, or revision choice affects the reader.

answer.answertext: A draft with comments still visible.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Draft comments weaken final readiness. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_Q03
question.questiontext:
Question ID: CW_U06_L07_Q03

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.01

A portfolio statement discusses voice. Which evidence best matches it?

answer.answertext: A random image pasted beside the title.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. This does not show voice development. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: A file name with no writing attached.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. A file name is not craft evidence.

answer.answertext: A paragraph saying the writer worked hard.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Effort alone does not show voice. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: A revised story excerpt where dialogue and sentence rhythm reveal character voice.
answer.feedback: Correct. This answer is supported by MLA.CW.PUB.01 because it selects a specific craft move or revision decision: "A revised story excerpt where dialogue and sentence rhythm reveal character voice.". That choice matches the prompt instead of giving a vague reaction, an unsupported preference, or a detail outside the draft. Use the same reasoning when you explain how a word, structure, voice, image, or revision choice affects the reader.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_Q04
question.questiontext:
Question ID: CW_U06_L07_Q04

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.COM.01

Which portfolio order has the clearest purpose?

answer.answertext: Alphabetical by file name with no explanation.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. This may not guide craft understanding. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: Story first for revised dialogue, poem second for voice through rhythm, statement last to explain growth.
answer.feedback: Correct. This answer is supported by MLA.CW.COM.01 because it selects a specific craft move or revision decision: "Story first for revised dialogue, poem second for voice through rhythm, statement last to explain growth.". That choice matches the prompt instead of giving a vague reaction, an unsupported preference, or a detail outside the draft. Use the same reasoning when you explain how a word, structure, voice, image, or revision choice affects the reader.

answer.answertext: Random order based on download time.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Random order does not support readers. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: Longest to shortest only because length matters most.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Length is not the main purpose. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_Q05
question.questiontext:
Question ID: CW_U06_L07_Q05

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.01

Which note is most useful during a readiness pass?

answer.answertext: Fix it later.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. This is too vague. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: Maybe change something.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. This does not identify the problem. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: Preview script and make character labels consistent.
answer.feedback: Correct. This answer is supported by MLA.CW.PUB.01 because it selects a specific craft move or revision decision: "Preview script and make character labels consistent.". That choice matches the prompt instead of giving a vague reaction, an unsupported preference, or a detail outside the draft. Use the same reasoning when you explain how a word, structure, voice, image, or revision choice affects the reader.

answer.answertext: It looks fine from far away.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Readiness requires specific checks. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_Q06
question.questiontext:
Question ID: CW_U06_L07_Q06

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.COM.01

How should an author statement connect to selected pieces?

answer.answertext: It should name skills the reader can see in the portfolio.
answer.feedback: Correct. This answer is supported by MLA.CW.COM.01 because it selects a specific craft move or revision decision: "It should name skills the reader can see in the portfolio.". That choice matches the prompt instead of giving a vague reaction, an unsupported preference, or a detail outside the draft. Use the same reasoning when you explain how a word, structure, voice, image, or revision choice affects the reader.

answer.answertext: It should discuss unrelated goals only.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. The statement should connect to the work.

answer.answertext: It should hide all revision evidence.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Revision evidence supports growth. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: It should replace the creative pieces.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. It explains the pieces; it does not replace them.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_Q07
question.questiontext:
Question ID: CW_U06_L07_Q07

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.01

Which presentation choice best supports the portfolio?

answer.answertext: Read the longest excerpt regardless of purpose.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Excerpt choice should be focused. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: Avoid explaining the excerpt.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. The presentation needs craft reasoning. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: Summarize every assignment from the course.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. That is too broad. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: Choose one excerpt that shows a craft choice connected to portfolio growth.
answer.feedback: Correct. This answer is supported by MLA.CW.PUB.01 because it selects a specific craft move or revision decision: "Choose one excerpt that shows a craft choice connected to portfolio growth.". That choice matches the prompt instead of giving a vague reaction, an unsupported preference, or a detail outside the draft. Use the same reasoning when you explain how a word, structure, voice, image, or revision choice affects the reader.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_Q08
question.questiontext:
Question ID: CW_U06_L07_Q08

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.COM.01

Which problem should be fixed before final publication?

answer.answertext: The writer can explain the piece clearly.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. That is a strength, not a problem.

answer.answertext: The final file includes bracketed notes that say add ending later.
answer.feedback: Correct. This answer is supported by MLA.CW.COM.01 because it selects a specific craft move or revision decision: "The final file includes bracketed notes that say add ending later.". That choice matches the prompt instead of giving a vague reaction, an unsupported preference, or a detail outside the draft. Use the same reasoning when you explain how a word, structure, voice, image, or revision choice affects the reader.

answer.answertext: The portfolio has a clear title.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. A clear title supports readiness. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: The author statement names revision growth.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. That supports synthesis. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_Q09
question.questiontext:
Question ID: CW_U06_L07_Q09

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.01

What makes a portfolio integrated?

answer.answertext: The files are unrelated but colorful.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Visual decoration does not create integration. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: The portfolio has no explanation.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Author reasoning is needed. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: The selected pieces, statement, revision evidence, and presentation plan connect to shared growth.
answer.feedback: Correct. This answer is supported by MLA.CW.PUB.01 because it selects a specific craft move or revision decision: "The selected pieces, statement, revision evidence, and presentation plan connect to shared growth.". That choice matches the prompt instead of giving a vague reaction, an unsupported preference, or a detail outside the draft. Use the same reasoning when you explain how a word, structure, voice, image, or revision choice affects the reader.

answer.answertext: The presentation ignores the pieces.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. The presentation should connect to the portfolio.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_Q10
question.questiontext:
Question ID: CW_U06_L07_Q10

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.COM.01

Which answer best explains reader effect?

answer.answertext: I put this first because I found it first.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. This does not explain reader effect. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: I added random spacing.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Random spacing does not support readers. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: I like the color.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Preference is not reader effect. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: I revised the line breaks so the reader pauses before the speaker's decision.
answer.feedback: Correct. This answer is supported by MLA.CW.COM.01 because it selects a specific craft move or revision decision: "I revised the line breaks so the reader pauses before the speaker's decision.". That choice matches the prompt instead of giving a vague reaction, an unsupported preference, or a detail outside the draft. Use the same reasoning when you explain how a word, structure, voice, image, or revision choice affects the reader.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_Q11
question.questiontext:
Question ID: CW_U06_L07_Q11

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.01

A student marks "needs revision" beside the presentation plan. What should come next?

answer.answertext: Write the exact missing action, such as add listening focus.
answer.feedback: Correct. This answer is supported by MLA.CW.PUB.01 because it selects a specific craft move or revision decision: "Write the exact missing action, such as add listening focus.". That choice matches the prompt instead of giving a vague reaction, an unsupported preference, or a detail outside the draft. Use the same reasoning when you explain how a word, structure, voice, image, or revision choice affects the reader.

answer.answertext: Ignore the note.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. The issue should be resolved. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: Delete the portfolio.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. One issue does not require deleting everything.

answer.answertext: Submit without checking.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Readiness requires follow-through. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_Q12
question.questiontext:
Question ID: CW_U06_L07_Q12

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.COM.01

Which choice shows revision evidence?

answer.answertext: A blank page.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. There is no evidence. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: A final piece with no explanation and no draft trail.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. This may not show revision evidence. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: A draft and final version with a note explaining how feedback improved dialogue.
answer.feedback: Correct. This answer is supported by MLA.CW.COM.01 because it selects a specific craft move or revision decision: "A draft and final version with a note explaining how feedback improved dialogue.". That choice matches the prompt instead of giving a vague reaction, an unsupported preference, or a detail outside the draft. Use the same reasoning when you explain how a word, structure, voice, image, or revision choice affects the reader.

answer.answertext: A decoration folder.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Decoration is not revision evidence. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_Q13
question.questiontext:
Question ID: CW_U06_L07_Q13

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.01

Which author rationale is strongest?

answer.answertext: I included this because it was easy.
answer.feedback: Incorrect. Ease is not a strong rationale. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.answertext: I included this poem because revising the image pattern made the speaker's change clearer.
answer.feedback: Correct. This answer is supported by MLA.CW.PUB.01 because it selects a specific craft move or revision decision: "I included this poem because revising the image pattern made the speaker's change clearer.". That choice matches the prompt instead of giving a vague reaction, an unsupported preference, or a detail outside the draft. question.name: CW_U02_PRE_R_Q01
question.questiontext: “For three weeks, Lena practiced her request on the walk home. Now she stood at the office door. She raised her hand to knock, then lowered it.” Why does the writer shift from summary to scene?

answer.answertext: To give each of the three weeks equal narrative attention.
To reveal the thoughts of the person inside the office.
To compress repeated preparation and slow down a moment of uncertain action.
To move backward from the office visit to an earlier memory.

question.name: CW_U02_PRE_R_Q02
question.questiontext: A scene ends with a storm flooding the bridge. The next scene begins with Mara taking a longer route to school the following morning. Which transition most clearly establishes both time and cause without adding an unsupported event?

answer.answertext: The next morning, with the bridge still flooded, Mara took the ridge road.
Meanwhile, Mara took the ridge road to school.
Years earlier, Mara had learned the ridge road by heart.
Because her friend had invited her, Mara took the ridge road.

question.name: CW_U02_PRE_R_Q03
question.questiontext: A story stays in third-person limited viewpoint through Imani: “Imani watched Tomas tuck the letter into his coat.” Which next sentence preserves that limited access?

answer.answertext: Tomas secretly hoped she would never ask about the letter.
Imani wondered whether he was hiding bad news.
Neither of them knew the letter would change their lives next winter.
Across town, his sister regretted sending the letter.

question.name: CW_U02_PRE_R_Q04
question.questiontext: Nora must return a borrowed violin before the last ferry leaves. At the dock, the gate is locked and the departure bell begins to ring. How does the setting contribute to the scene?

answer.answertext: It replaces Nora's immediate goal with a description of the harbor.
It resolves the conflict by explaining why the violin was borrowed.
It gives Nora unlimited time to decide what to do.
It combines a physical obstacle and a deadline that restrict Nora's choices.

question.name: CW_U02_PRE_R_Q05
question.questiontext: Early in a story, Eli checks the locked garden gate each evening. In the final scene, he props that same gate open and sets out a second chair. Which interpretation best accounts for the changed recurring detail?

answer.answertext: The changed gate and added chair suggest movement from guarded separation toward welcome.
The repetition establishes that Eli's attitude has remained entirely unchanged.
The open gate proves that Eli has permanently resolved every conflict.
The gate means freedom solely because gates always have that fixed meaning.

question.name: CW_U02_PRE_R_Q06
question.questiontext: “I never cared about winning,” the narrator insists. Later, the narrator describes secretly replacing a rival's entry card with a blank one. How should a reader evaluate the narrator's claim?

answer.answertext: Accept it because first-person narrators necessarily understand their own motives accurately.
Conclude that every physical event the narrator describes must also be false.
Question the self-description because the reported action contradicts indifference to winning.
Treat the contradiction as proof that the story has changed to omniscient narration.

question.name: CW_U02_PRE_R_Q07
question.questiontext: The reader sees a thief hide beneath a desk. A guard enters, glances around, and says, “At last, a room where nothing can surprise me.” The guard has not seen the thief. What creates dramatic irony here?

answer.answertext: The guard deliberately says the opposite of what the guard believes.
The thief's hiding place makes the outcome certain to every character.
The narrator directly announces a general lesson about honesty.
The reader knows about a danger that the confident guard does not recognize.

question.name: CW_U02_PRE_R_Q08
question.questiontext: A fictional town creates a Committee for Faster Decisions. Before answering any request, its members must hold twelve meetings to approve the agenda for a thirteenth. What is the clearest target of this satire?

answer.answertext: The idea that citizens should ever have a voice in public decisions.
Procedures that claim to improve efficiency but instead delay useful action.
The personal appearance of the individual committee members.
The belief that all careful discussion leads to faster decisions.

question.name: CW_U02_PRE_R_Q09
question.questiontext: A writer wants to prolong uncertainty immediately before a character opens an examination-result envelope. Which revision best serves that purpose?

answer.answertext: Summarize opening the envelope and celebrating the result in one sentence.
Reveal the result first, then list unrelated events from the character's childhood.
Expand the brief hesitation into the thumb catching under the flap and a pause before the paper tears.
Replace the envelope scene with a general explanation of how examinations are marked.

question.name: CW_U02_PRE_R_Q10
question.questiontext: A scene's goal is to move two friends from mistrust toward cautious cooperation. They must carry a fragile model through a narrow doorway together. Which ending best integrates the setting, their actions, and a meaningful change?

answer.answertext: After a tense pause, one asks the other to guide the back edge; they lift on the same count, though neither apologizes yet.
They leave the model untouched and repeat their original accusations without any change in their choices.
The narrator declares their friendship repaired while they refuse to touch the model or speak to each other.
A teacher carries the model out while the friends continue avoiding one another exactly as before.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q01
question.questiontext: "The apartment smelled like rain and burnt toast. Nia placed her college envelope beside the sink and waited for Grandma to notice." How do the domestic setting details work with the envelope?

answer.answertext: They suggest that the envelope concerns a minor household repair.
They establish that the narrator already knows Grandma will approve.
They contrast an important personal development with ordinary domestic life.
They show Grandma noticing the envelope before Nia places it down.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q02
question.questiontext: "You tell yourself the stage lights are too bright to see anyone, but you still find your father's empty seat." What effect does second person create?

answer.answertext: It draws the reader into the character's self-address and conflicting attention.
It gives direct access to the absent father's private thoughts.
It establishes that the narrator speaks for every audience member.
It creates the distance of an observer who cannot report inner experience.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q03
question.questiontext: A writer wants to show that a character is becoming more honest. Which action best supports that purpose?

answer.answertext: The character rehearses an easier version of the story and keeps it unchanged.
The character crosses out a false sentence and writes the harder truth beneath it.
The character makes the false account sound more convincing.
The character hides the page so nobody can question its accuracy.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q04
question.questiontext: "The bike chain slipped again at the bottom of the hill. Omar looked up at the hospital windows and started pushing." What does the action reveal?

answer.answertext: Omar abandons his destination as soon as progress becomes difficult.
Omar values repairing the bicycle more than reaching the hospital.
Omar has reached the hospital and is now remembering the journey.
Omar adapts his action to an obstacle because reaching the destination matters.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q05
question.questiontext: A draft uses a full page of backstory before the character enters the contest room. The unit skill focus is narrative scene development. What revision best improves pacing?

answer.answertext: Begin closer to the contest-room decision and weave essential background into the action.
Keep all the backstory together and delay the contest until the last sentence.
Expand the travel history even when it does not affect the contest decision.
Replace the decision with a summary of the contest rules.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q06
question.questiontext: "I said I did not care who won, but I checked the scoreboard before I checked my ankle." What does the narrator's behavior show?

answer.answertext: The narrator's claim and behavior consistently establish indifference.
The action proves the ankle injury is imaginary.
The priority given to the scoreboard undermines the claim of not caring.
The contradiction gives the reader direct access to every competitor's thoughts.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q07
question.questiontext: "The garden gate hung open, and the tomatoes lay crushed under one set of muddy footprints." Which technique is strongest?

answer.answertext: A flashback directly explains who damaged the garden.
Concrete setting details imply a disturbance before its cause is explained.
Dialogue reveals the intruder's motive.
An omniscient narrator explicitly states the gardener's private thoughts.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q08
question.questiontext: Which choice best states how point of view supports narrative meaning?

answer.answertext: Point of view determines whether a narrative must use short sentences.
Point of view ensures every character receives equal narrative attention.
Point of view prevents writers from withholding information.
Point of view controls access to information and the reader's closeness to experience.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q09
question.questiontext: "Mara kept the receipt for the returned dress taped inside her locker." What question would most help revise the detail for meaning?

answer.answertext: What desire, memory, or conflict makes Mara preserve proof of the return?
Could the receipt be described in greater detail without considering Mara's reason?
Could every locker receive the same amount of description as the receipt?
Could the detail be replaced by a list of all the items Mara has purchased?

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q10
question.questiontext: Scene purpose: show a character deciding to speak up. Which ending best completes the arc?

answer.answertext: The character lowers their hand and waits for someone else to say what matters.
The character hears the room go quiet and says the first true sentence aloud.
The character leaves the meeting before having to make a choice.
The character repeats the intention to speak but takes no new action.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q11
question.questiontext: "The necklace clicked against the microphone as Priya leaned forward." Which integrated effect is strongest if Priya is about to confess?

answer.answertext: It explains exactly why Priya has decided to confess.
It shifts attention away from Priya's immediate action to an unrelated memory.
It makes a small sound conspicuous at a tense public moment.
It establishes that everyone already knows what Priya will confess.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q12
question.questiontext: Leo first says he found a match on the sidewalk. In a later account of the same fire, he says he was holding it. Neither account is independently confirmed. What is the most defensible conclusion?

answer.answertext: The changing account gives reason to question Leo's reliability without proving his exact motive.
The changing account proves each version is equally accurate.
The detail establishes an intentional shift to the listener's private thoughts.
The changing account proves the match caused no harm.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q13
question.questiontext: A student writes, "The room was nice. The person was sad. The thing mattered." What revision would best improve craft?

answer.answertext: Replace the vague adjectives with stronger adjectives while leaving the situation unspecified.
Add a second paragraph that repeats the same emotional labels.
Explain that the object is important without showing its connection to the character.
Choose specific actions and details that connect the person, object, and intended effect.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q14
question.questiontext: "The train pulled away before Elena reached the platform. She laughed, then covered her mouth with both hands." What does the reaction suggest?

answer.answertext: The laughter proves Elena feels only uncomplicated happiness.
The shift from laughter to covering her mouth suggests a reaction that is not simple or fully explained.
The gesture establishes exactly whom Elena blames for the missed train.
The reaction proves Elena intended to miss the train all along.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q15
question.questiontext: Which option best defines an integrated narrative scene?

answer.answertext: A scene that includes every available technique whether or not it serves the action.
A scene that gives equal space to every object in its setting.
A scene whose viewpoint, character choices, setting, pacing, and details support a coherent purpose.
A scene that explains its theme instead of letting choices and consequences develop it.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q16
question.questiontext: "The room went silent after I said the name. Even the aquarium filter seemed to stop." What does the aquarium detail do?

answer.answertext: It makes the silence feel pervasive by focusing on a normally audible sound.
It establishes that the filter has certainly suffered a mechanical failure.
It explains the entire history associated with the spoken name.
It shifts the focal viewpoint into the thoughts of another person.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q17
question.questiontext: A character needs to admit damaging a borrowed instrument before its owner leaves the rehearsal hall. Which revision best makes the setting pressure the character's choice?

answer.answertext: Remove the closing-time limit so the character can avoid making a choice.
Describe the wall color at length without connecting it to the character's goal.
Explain the character's childhood but omit what the character does now.
Let the closing announcement force the character to choose between confessing now and losing the chance.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q18
question.questiontext: "Third-person limited follows Jade as she waits outside the office." What can the reader usually know?

answer.answertext: The unspoken motives of everyone Jade encounters, presented as facts.
Jade's thoughts and perceptions, while others' motives remain observed or inferred.
Only externally visible movement, with no access to Jade's inner experience.
The reader's actions addressed directly through the pronoun you.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q19
question.questiontext: "The empty chair at the end of the table stayed pulled out all dinner." What does the detail most likely suggest?

answer.answertext: The detail proves the absent person will arrive later that evening.
The detail proves the diners have fully resolved the absence.
The sustained place for someone missing suggests absence matters to the meal.
The detail identifies the precise reason the person is absent.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q20
question.questiontext: A draft has the line, "I was nervous." Which revision best shows rather than only tells?

answer.answertext: I counted the same three floor tiles until my name was called.
I felt extremely nervous about hearing my name.
My nervousness was intense and difficult to describe.
I knew that nervousness was what I was experiencing.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q21
question.questiontext: "The narrator refuses to explain why she hides the medal, but she checks the drawer every night." What is the best reader inference?

answer.answertext: The narrator has become entirely indifferent to the medal.
The repeated checking suggests emotional investment despite concealment.
The narrator's silence proves the medal was stolen.
The checking reveals precisely why the medal is being hidden.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q22
question.questiontext: Which feedback best helps a student whose scene has many details but no clear purpose?

answer.answertext: Make each detail longer before deciding what the scene should accomplish.
Remove every concrete detail so the purpose can be stated abstractly.
Identify the scene's main change and revise details according to how they support it.
Add a new technique to every paragraph regardless of its effect.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q23
question.questiontext: "When the principal asked who painted the mural, Sam looked at the blue stain on his sleeve." What does the stain do?

answer.answertext: It proves Sam acted alone and had no permission to paint.
It gives the principal direct access to Sam's private thoughts.
It resolves Sam's motive without requiring any further evidence.
It supplies a concrete clue connecting Sam to the mural without explaining the whole situation.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q24
question.questiontext: "The doorbell rang once. Nobody moved. It rang again, and Aunt Celia set down the carving knife." What pacing technique is used?

answer.answertext: Repeated ringing and delayed response stretch the wait before action.
A broad summary compresses many evenings into a sentence.
A flashback moves from the present room to an earlier dinner.
An explanatory aside resolves the identity of the visitor immediately.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q25
question.questiontext: Which final revision question best prepares a scene for unit mastery?

answer.answertext: Have I made every scene equally slow regardless of its purpose?
Have I included a separate example of every technique even when distracting?
Have I explained each symbol so no interpretation remains possible?
Do viewpoint, choices, setting, pacing, and significant details work together toward the intended effect?

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q26
question.questiontext: Which choice best identifies a narrative technique in this sentence? "Maya pressed her ear to the door and held her breath."

answer.answertext: Dialogue that reveals a conflict through spoken words.
Reflection that explains what an earlier event means.
Physical action that can suggest attention or tension.
A temporal transition that moves the narrative to a later day.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q27
question.questiontext: Which revision best turns the event list into a scene? Event list: "I opened the box. I saw the medal. I cried."

answer.answertext: I opened the box, saw the medal, and cried.
I lifted the cardboard flap and found the silver medal wrapped in a blue ribbon. For a moment, I could not move. Then my eyes filled with tears.
First I opened the box; next I saw the medal; finally I cried.
Opening the box caused an emotional response because the medal was important.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q28
question.questiontext: Which transition best shows cause in this sentence? "_____ the hallway lights went out, Jordan reached for the wall."

answer.answertext: Because
Although
Before
Even if

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q29
question.questiontext: Which sentence is written in first person point of view?

answer.answertext: Lena opened the drawer and held her breath.
She opened the drawer and held her breath.
I opened the drawer and held my breath.
You open the drawer and hold your breath.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q30
question.questiontext: Which choice correctly explains third person limited point of view?

answer.answertext: The narrator uses I to recount personal experience.
The narrator moves freely among all characters' unspoken thoughts.
The narrator reports only outward behavior and never any inner experience.
The narrator uses names or third-person pronouns while filtering experience through one character.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q31
question.questiontext: "Mina kept the bent bus pass in her coat pocket even after she moved close enough to walk to school." Which key element is most important?

answer.answertext: An exchange of dialogue that states Mina's motive.
A retained object whose significance extends beyond its practical use.
A full summary explaining every stage of Mina's move.
An explicit shift into another character's consciousness.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q32
question.questiontext: "The room was empty except for a chair turned toward the wall." Which response best distinguishes the detail's possible effect from an unsupported explanation?

answer.answertext: The isolated chair and its unusual orientation can create uncertainty without establishing an exact cause.
The chair proves a specific violent event occurred in the room.
The chair establishes the identity and motive of the previous occupant.
The description directly explains how every character feels about the room.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q33
question.questiontext: "I set the cracked mug beside the new one and reached for the cracked one again." What is the literal meaning?

answer.answertext: The narrator rejects all connections with the past.
The narrator has decided to give away both mugs.
The narrator reaches again for the cracked mug rather than the new one.
The narrator is certainly angry with the person who bought the new mug.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q34
question.questiontext: "The graduation banner stretched across the living room, but the suitcase by the stairs was already packed." Which evidence creates contrast?

answer.answertext: Both details explicitly show that the character refuses to leave.
The celebration suggested by the banner is placed beside the departure suggested by the suitcase.
The packed suitcase proves the graduation celebration was canceled.
The banner explains exactly how the person leaving feels about the departure.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q35
question.questiontext: "I was clearly the calmest person in the room. True, I had knocked over two chairs and shouted at the clock, but that only proved everyone else was making me nervous." What creates irony?

answer.answertext: The narrator's actions fully support the stated self-assessment.
The narrator clearly admits panic without trying to excuse it.
The passage gives another character's private judgment directly.
The claim of calmness conflicts with behavior and excuses that suggest agitation.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q36
question.questiontext: "To prove our club valued student voices, the officers created a suggestion box, locked it, lost the key, and congratulated themselves for listening." What is the satirical target?

answer.answertext: Leadership that advertises participation while preventing meaningful participation.
The inherent inability of students to offer useful suggestions.
The idea that every physical suggestion box is an ineffective invention.
The claim that listening carefully necessarily causes leaders to lose authority.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q37
question.questiontext: "The phone lit up. I reached for it, stopped, and watched the screen go dark again." Which pacing choice is used?

answer.answertext: A summary compresses several routine days into one sentence.
Small actions expand a brief moment of hesitation.
A flashback interrupts the present with a fully dramatized childhood event.
The result is revealed before the character has a chance to react.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q38
question.questiontext: A writer wants uncertainty about possible danger at the doorway. Which revision most clearly supports that purpose? Draft: "I opened the door."

answer.answertext: I opened the door and immediately learned that everything was safe.
I opened the door while recalling its exact purchase price.
I opened the door slowly; the last message still read, "Do not go inside yet."
I opened the door, then summarized an uneventful afternoon.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q39
question.questiontext: Maya stands outside the closed gym doors with the debate trophy under one arm. Inside, her teammates are laughing. She won the final round but ignored Kai's signal to let him answer. The writer wants success to be complicated by damaged trust. Which scene plan best integrates that purpose with viewpoint, detail, and pacing?

answer.answertext: Emphasize the win alone, move into every teammate's thoughts, and skip Maya's hesitation.
Describe the gym's construction at length without connecting it to Maya's decision.
Summarize the debate rules and end before Maya chooses whether to enter.
Stay close to Maya, let the trophy press against her side during her hesitation, and move into action when she decides to face Kai.

question.name: CW_U02_UA_R_Q40
question.questiontext: The narrator says, "I kept the cracked compass in my pocket because Dad said it always found the truth. When it spun wildly beside the old train station, I almost turned back." What is the strongest scene purpose?

answer.answertext: To show a character facing uncertainty through an object connected to a parent's advice.
To establish that the compass supplies an objectively reliable answer to the character's problem.
To resolve why the character has arrived at the station and exactly what will happen next.
To show the character has already rejected the father's influence and feels no hesitation.

question_category.name: CW U2 L1 Reviewed 2026-09-06
question_category.info: The default category for questions shared in context 'U2L1 Q'.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q01
question.questiontext: Which sentence uses action as the main narrative technique?

answer.answertext: I shoved the folded note into my jacket pocket before anyone saw it.
The porch smelled like rain and old wood.
"Do not open that," Reese whispered.
I wondered whether the note had been meant for me.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q02
question.questiontext: Which choice best explains the purpose of a transition in narrative writing?

answer.answertext: They make every event take the same amount of narrative space.
They replace the need to show a character reacting to events.
They clarify relationships between moments, such as time, place, or cause.
They explain every character motive before the action begins.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q03
question.questiontext: Which revision best changes a plain event list into a developed scene? Event list: "The door opened. I saw my cousin. I smiled."

answer.answertext: The door opened, I saw my cousin, and I smiled.
First the door opened. Next I saw my cousin. Finally I smiled.
I smiled because I saw my cousin after the door opened.
The door opened slowly, and my cousin stood there holding a backpack with both hands. For a second, neither of us moved. Then I smiled so hard my cheeks hurt.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q04
question.questiontext: Which sentence uses dialogue?

answer.answertext: Nia tapped the glass twice and waited.
"Is anyone in there?" Nia asked.
The glass was cold enough to fog beneath her fingers.
Nia wondered if anyone would answer.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q05
question.questiontext: Which transition best shows contrast?

answer.answertext: After dinner, Malik washed the trophy.
Because the trophy broke, Malik frowned.
Outside, the crowd cheered; inside, Malik stared at the broken trophy.
Beside the window, Malik set the trophy down.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q06
question.questiontext: A student writes, "Then I walked home. Then I opened the door. Then I saw the lights." What is the clearest revision advice?

answer.answertext: Choose transitions that identify the actual relationship, such as time, place, or cause.
Replace every Then with Later, regardless of the relationship between events.
Remove every transition even where the sequence would become unclear.
Add dialogue between each event without considering what it contributes.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q07
question.questiontext: Which choice is reflection?

answer.answertext: The hallway narrowed near the music room.
"Wait for me," I called.
I turned the corner and stopped.
I realized I had been hoping the letter would never arrive.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q08
question.questiontext: Which sentence uses description to develop mood?

answer.answertext: I knocked three times.
The hallway light flickered over the peeling green paint.
"Come in," she said.
I understood why she sounded afraid.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q09
question.questiontext: A writer wants to dramatize a frightening moment, but the draft reads: "The dog barked. Then I ran. Then I hid." What revision need is most important for that purpose?

answer.answertext: The sequence cannot be understood because no events are named.
The scene already contains more dialogue than action.
The event list needs selected actions, perceptions, or reactions that develop the important moment.
The description interrupts the action with too many sensory details.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q10
question.questiontext: Which transition best shows time?

answer.answertext: Under the bench, my ticket curled at the edge.
Because I had forgotten my ticket, I could not board.
Even though I was nervous, I stepped forward.
Before sunrise, the bus station was nearly empty.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q11
question.questiontext: Which choice best explains why dialogue should be used intentionally?

answer.answertext: Use speech to reveal character, conflict, relationships, or information that matters to the scene.
Use speech mainly to restate what the narration has already made clear.
Use speech to list background facts even when the speakers already know them.
Use speech whenever a time transition would otherwise be needed.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q12
question.questiontext: Which transition best shows cause and effect?

answer.answertext: Across the room, the curtain moved.
Meanwhile, the hallway stayed quiet.
Since the window was open, the papers slid off the desk.
Later, the papers were gone.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q13
question.questiontext: Which version most clearly uses action to show nervousness?

answer.answertext: I was very nervous.
I twisted the bracelet around my wrist until the clasp pinched my skin.
Nervousness is uncomfortable.
The room was blue and quiet.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q14
question.questiontext: "The scent of oranges carried me back to the kitchen where my grandmother taught me to peel them." What connects the present moment to the memory?

answer.answertext: A stated passage of several hours.
A move into another character's thoughts.
An explicit explanation of a future consequence.
An association between a present sensation and a remembered experience.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q15
question.questiontext: Which explanation best matches the revision? Draft: "I dropped the cup. Everyone stared." Revision: "When the cup hit the tile, the room went silent. A ring of coffee spread around my shoes while every face turned toward me."

answer.answertext: The time connection and concrete description make the moment easier to follow and imagine.
The revision compresses the whole event into less narrative time.
The revision replaces a physical event with an explanation of its theme.
The revision shifts the event into another character's private thoughts.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q16
question.questiontext: Which sentence uses reflection?

answer.answertext: The elevator doors opened on the sixth floor.
"Are you coming?" Dad asked.
I knew then that I had not come to apologize; I had come to say goodbye.
A red suitcase leaned against the wall.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q17
question.questiontext: Which transition best shows place?

answer.answertext: After the bell rang, Mia stayed seated.
At the far end of the hallway, Mia spotted the blue locker.
Because the hallway was crowded, Mia waited.
Even though she was late, Mia smiled.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q18
question.questiontext: What should a writer do before choosing narrative techniques for a scene?

answer.answertext: Which technique could I repeat most often throughout the draft?
Which details could I expand without considering their relevance?
How can I give every moment equal space?
What should the reader experience or understand at this moment?

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q19
question.questiontext: Which choice best revises "The room was scary" using description?

answer.answertext: The only light came from the hallway, and the closet door clicked softly in the dark.
The room was very, very scary.
I was scared because the room was scary.
The room was a room in a building.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q20
question.questiontext: Which statement about transitions is accurate?

answer.answertext: Transitions signal chronology but cannot connect causes or contrasts.
Transitions must appear at the beginning of every sentence.
Transitions can clarify time, place, cause, contrast, sequence, or a shift of focus.
Transitions work best when the same connector is used for every relationship.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q21
question.questiontext: Which sentence best uses dialogue to reveal conflict?

answer.answertext: "Hello," I said.
"The weather is nice," she said.
"I brought my notebook," he said.
"You promised you would not tell her," I said.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q22
question.questiontext: Which choice best identifies the transition in this sentence? "Although the hallway was crowded, I could still hear my name from the office."

answer.answertext: Time
Contrast
Place
Cause

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q23
question.questiontext: A writer wants readers to experience a character's embarrassment through a scene rather than an emotional summary. Which sentence most needs revision for that purpose?

answer.answertext: I was embarrassed, worried, and upset about the mistake.
My pencil rolled off the desk and tapped against the silent floor.
"Please do not read that out loud," I whispered.
Around me, every chair scraped back at once.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q24
question.questiontext: In a draft, a character is searching a room for a missing letter. The next sentence says, "She left." Readers cannot tell why she stopped searching. Which revision advice best addresses that gap?

answer.answertext: Replace left with departed; the reason will then be clear.
Show the discovery that causes the departure and connect it to the action.
Describe the room's furniture in more detail before the departure.
Add three time markers but leave the reason for leaving unstated.

question.name: CW_U02_L01_R_Q25
question.questiontext: Which sentence best combines action and reflection?

answer.answertext: The gate was silver.
"Lock the gate," she said.
I locked the gate behind me and wondered whether leaving had made me brave or cruel.
I locked the gate.

question_category.name: CW U2 L2 Reviewed 2026-09-06
question_category.info: The default category for questions shared in context 'U2L2 Q'.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q01
question.questiontext: Which sentence is written in third person limited point of view?

answer.answertext: I slipped the key under my sleeve and hoped nobody noticed.
Dani hoped nobody noticed the key; Leo privately hoped she would drop it.
Dani slipped the key under her sleeve and hoped nobody noticed.
The key was silver and cold beneath the light.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q02
question.questiontext: Which question should a writer ask first when checking point of view?

answer.answertext: Who narrates, and whose knowledge or perceptions limit the account?
How can every character receive an equal number of sentences?
How can I replace every name with a pronoun?
How can I reveal the ending before choosing a narrator?

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q03
question.questiontext: Which sentence is first person?

answer.answertext: She kept her hand on the envelope until the bell rang.
I kept my hand on the envelope until the bell rang.
Mara kept her hand on the envelope until the bell rang.
They kept their hands on the envelope until the bell rang.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q04
question.questiontext: In a first-person scene, Omar has not explained his feelings, and the narrator has no later information. Which sentence asserts Omar's private state as certain rather than observing or inferring it?

answer.answertext: I saw Omar glance at the clock.
I thought Omar looked worried.
I heard Omar whisper my name.
I knew Omar regretted every word he had said.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q05
question.questiontext: Which statement best explains narrative distance?

answer.answertext: Narrative distance is how close or far the narration feels from a character's thoughts and emotions.
Narrative distance is the number of miles between characters.
Narrative distance is the length of a paragraph.
Narrative distance is the order of events in a plot.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q06
question.questiontext: Which revision keeps third person limited focused on Tessa? Draft: "Tessa opened the message. Eli felt relieved because she had not seen the last line."

answer.answertext: Tessa opened the message. Eli felt relieved because she had not seen the last line.
Tessa opened the message. Eli thought she had not seen the last line.
Tessa opened the message. Across the room, Eli released a slow breath when her eyes stopped before the last line.
Tessa opened the message, and Eli knew she had not seen the last line.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q07
question.questiontext: Which choice is an example of third person omniscient point of view?

answer.answertext: I hid the ticket and waited by the stairs.
Rae feared losing the ticket; Jonah, unaware of her fear, privately hoped she would leave it behind.
Rae hid the ticket under the stairs and held her breath.
Under the stairs, the ticket bent at one corner.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q08
question.questiontext: A first-person narrator has not been told how Lila feels. Which sentence suggests fear through evidence available to the narrator rather than claiming direct access to her mind?

answer.answertext: I knew Lila was terrified of what I would say.
Lila was terrified of what I would say.
Lila knew I would ruin everything.
Lila's voice cracked when she asked what I had heard.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q09
question.questiontext: The writer intends a first-person account limited to what the narrator observes in this moment. Which sentence consistently preserves that access?

answer.answertext: I opened the locker, and Maya stepped back without saying a word.
I opened the locker, and Maya wondered why I looked guilty.
I opened the locker, and Maya was secretly angry.
I opened the locker, and Maya knew the truth.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q10
question.questiontext: How does first person point of view often affect a story?

answer.answertext: It guarantees that the narrator's interpretation is accurate.
It can create closeness while limiting readers to the narrator's experience and account.
It requires narration to remain distant from emotion.
It gives direct access to unreported private thoughts of other characters.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q11
question.questiontext: A passage uses she but stays within Mira's perceptions. Which distinction best explains this design?

answer.answertext: The use of third-person pronouns alone proves unrestricted knowledge.
A sentence can reveal every mind as long as it avoids names.
Grammatical person identifies the pronouns; focalization identifies whose perception filters the scene.
Focalization is the physical distance between two characters.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q12
question.questiontext: Which sentence best shows third person limited with close narrative distance?

answer.answertext: Mira stared at the clock and wished she could stop the minute hand with her eyes.
The room was square and quiet.
People moved through the room.
A clock hung above the door.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q13
question.questiontext: A scene is meant to stay within one first-person narrator's present knowledge, but a sentence states another character's unspoken thought as fact. Which revision best repairs that access problem?

answer.answertext: Change the first-person pronouns but keep both characters' private thoughts.
Add sensory adjectives to the sentence that enters the other mind.
Delete the character's name but retain the claim about their hidden thought.
Replace the unsupported private thought with behavior, dialogue, or an explicitly marked inference available to the narrator.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q14
question.questiontext: Which choice correctly describes third person limited?

answer.answertext: A character narrates using I.
The narrator uses third person pronouns while staying close to one character's experience.
The narrator has no access to any character's thoughts.
The narrator reveals every character's private thoughts equally.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q15
question.questiontext: Which sentence is most likely third person omniscient?

answer.answertext: I held the photograph against my chest.
Leah held the photograph and tried not to cry.
Leah wished Sam would call; across town, Sam privately resolved never to call again.
The photograph curled at the edge.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q16
question.questiontext: Which revision best changes first person to third person limited? Original: "I waited outside the office and wished I had told the truth earlier."

answer.answertext: Marcus waited outside the office and wished he had told the truth earlier.
I waited outside the office and wished I had told the truth earlier.
Marcus waited outside the office, and Ms. Li knew he had lied.
Waiting happened outside the office.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q17
question.questiontext: The intended viewpoint is third-person limited through Ava. Draft: "Ava opened the notebook. She wondered who had written in it. Across the room, Ben knew the answer." Which part violates that intended limit?

answer.answertext: It creates distance by removing all access to inner experience.
It changes the grammatical person from third to first.
It reports only actions Ava can observe.
It enters Ben's private knowledge after establishing Ava as the limited viewpoint.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q18
question.questiontext: Which choice best explains why point of view affects reader trust?

answer.answertext: A first-person pronoun guarantees a truthful account.
A narrator selects and frames information, so readers compare claims with evidence.
Using third person removes all possibility of bias.
Close narrative distance proves the narrator understands everyone correctly.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q19
question.questiontext: Which sentence best keeps third person limited focused on Devon?

answer.answertext: Devon heard the drawer open, and Mia hoped he would not turn around.
Devon heard the drawer open, and Mia knew he was afraid.
Devon heard the drawer open behind him and wished he had locked it.
Devon heard the drawer open, and everyone in the house felt nervous.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q20
question.questiontext: Which point of view is used here? "We waited behind the curtain until the principal called our names."

answer.answertext: First person
Third person limited
Third person omniscient
Objective third person

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q21
question.questiontext: "Mira read the notice. Another delay. Of course the office had found a way to waste her afternoon." The last two sentences carry Mira's judgment without quotation marks or she thought. Which technique is used?

answer.answertext: A direct quotation spoken aloud to another character.
Free indirect style, blending third-person narration with Mira's judgment.
An omniscient report of several characters' private thoughts.
An objective report that excludes a character's evaluation.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q22
question.questiontext: Which sentence best avoids directly naming another character's private thought in first person?

answer.answertext: I knew Theo regretted giving me the card.
Theo regretted giving me the card.
Theo knew I would keep the card forever.
Theo stared at the card in my hand and rubbed the corner of the envelope.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q23
question.questiontext: Which statement is true about first person narration?

answer.answertext: It automatically includes all characters' unspoken thoughts.
It cannot report information obtained through dialogue.
It is limited to what the narrator experiences, learns, remembers, or infers, rather than automatic access to other minds.
It must describe events without offering any interpretation.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q24
question.questiontext: The writer intends a first-person account with no access to Carlos's unspoken thoughts. Which revision preserves that limit? Draft: "I followed Carlos into the gym. He hoped nobody would notice the envelope."

answer.answertext: I followed Carlos into the gym. He hoped nobody would notice the envelope.
I followed Carlos into the gym, and he hoped privately.
Carlos hoped nobody would notice the envelope while I followed him.
I followed Carlos into the gym. He kept one hand over the envelope and avoided looking at the ticket table.

question.name: CW_U02_L02_R_Q25
question.questiontext: Which explanation best connects point of view to voice?

answer.answertext: Narrative position and access shape diction, attitude, and the distance readers feel.
Changing narrator access necessarily leaves the voice unchanged.
Voice depends on dialogue punctuation rather than narrative perspective.
First-person narration requires the same attitude in every story.

question_category.name: CW U2 L3 Reviewed 2026-09-06
question_category.info: The default category for questions shared in context 'U2L3 Q'.

question.name: CW_U02_L03_R_Q01
question.questiontext: Passage: "The mailbox leaned toward the road, its red flag stuck halfway up." Which key element is doing craft work?

answer.answertext: Setting detail
Dialogue
Point of view shift
Direct explanation

question.name: CW_U02_L03_R_Q02
question.questiontext: Passage: "Every time the coach asked for volunteers, Nia retied the same shoelace." What does the repeated action suggest?

answer.answertext: The action proves she has decided to volunteer.
The action proves she dislikes the coach.
The repeated action may help her avoid attention or express nervousness.
The action establishes that her shoelace is certainly broken.

question.name: CW_U02_L03_R_Q03
question.questiontext: Which statement moves beyond labeling a key element?

answer.answertext: The gate is a setting element.
The passage mentions a gate before an argument.
The gate has a lock on it.
The locked gate turns the setting into an obstacle, restricting the character before the argument.

question.name: CW_U02_L03_R_Q04
question.questiontext: Passage: "Marta wore her brother's old jacket, though the sleeves stopped above her wrists." What is the strongest inference?

answer.answertext: The passage establishes the exact temperature.
Keeping a poorly fitting family garment may suggest attachment beyond its practical use.
The passage proves she resents her brother.
The garment tells us exactly why her brother is absent.

question.name: CW_U02_L03_R_Q05
question.questiontext: Passage: "The kitchen clock ticked louder than the rain while Marcus stood beside his zipped suitcase." Which pair of elements works together?

answer.answertext: Dialogue and satire
Theme and rhyme
Setting sound and object detail
Flashback and first person

question.name: CW_U02_L03_R_Q06
question.questiontext: Which detail would best reveal a character's hesitation without saying "she hesitated"?

answer.answertext: Her hand hovered over the send button, then dropped to her side.
She was hesitant.
She stood there.
Hesitation is difficult.

question.name: CW_U02_L03_R_Q07
question.questiontext: Passage: "The trophy sat behind the family photos, turned so its nameplate faced the wall." What does placement add?
