question.questiontext: Central idea: Hope can survive failure. Which detail supports it?

answer.answertext: The farmer burns every seed.
The field has dirt.
After the failed harvest, the farmer saves seeds for spring.
The calendar has dates.

question.name: CW_U03_L04_R_Q11
question.questiontext: Passage: Ana keeps rereading the invitation but never opens the door. Central idea: Fear can keep people from accepting connection. What detail supports it?

answer.answertext: The door is made of wood.
The invitation has ink.
Ana knows the alphabet.
Ana rereads the invitation but does not open the door.

question.name: CW_U03_L04_R_Q12
question.questiontext: What should a writer do with an interesting detail that does not support the central idea?

answer.answertext: Keep it no matter what.
Revise it so it supports the idea, or cut it.
Add ten more unrelated details.
Delete the central idea.

question.name: CW_U03_L04_R_Q13
question.questiontext: Central idea: Pride can prevent a person from learning. Which detail supports it?

answer.answertext: The character closes the instruction book after one page and says, "I already know."
The character studies carefully.
The character asks a mentor for advice.
The character admits confusion.

question.name: CW_U03_L04_R_Q14
question.questiontext: Passage: The narrator carries a cracked bowl into the new apartment because it belonged to her mother. Central idea: Memory can make change bearable. How does the bowl support it?

answer.answertext: The bowl proves nothing changes.
The bowl is unrelated because it is cracked.
The bowl carries memory into the new place.
The bowl only shows cooking instructions.

question.name: CW_U03_L04_R_Q15
question.questiontext: Which detail distracts from the central idea "honesty can repair harm"?

answer.answertext: The character admits the lie.
The character returns the hidden letter.
The character apologizes directly.
A full paragraph explains an unrelated video game level.

question.name: CW_U03_L04_R_Q16
question.questiontext: Central idea: Community support makes hardship easier to face. Which detail best supports it?

answer.answertext: Everyone closes their doors.
Neighbors take turns bringing meals after the fire.
The house has windows.
A clock ticks.

question.name: CW_U03_L04_R_Q17
question.questiontext: What does "development" mean in this lesson?

answer.answertext: The way an idea grows through story details and choices.
The number of pages only.
A random list of objects.
A title with no scene.

question.name: CW_U03_L04_R_Q18
question.questiontext: Central idea: Forgiveness can begin before trust is fully rebuilt. Which detail supports it?

answer.answertext: The character forgets the conflict entirely.
The character refuses any repair forever.
The character says, "I forgive you," but keeps the conversation short.
The character buys shoes.

question.name: CW_U03_L04_R_Q19
question.questiontext: Passage: Kai wants to be seen as brave, so he hides his shaking hands in his pockets before stepping forward. Central idea: Courage can exist beside fear. What detail supports it?

answer.answertext: Kai has pockets.
Kai never moves.
Kai feels no fear.
Kai steps forward while hiding shaking hands.

question.name: CW_U03_L04_R_Q20
question.questiontext: Which revision best supports "kindness can interrupt cruelty"?

answer.answertext: Add a character who changes the subject while classmates laugh.
Add a character who says, "Stop," and sits beside the student being mocked.
Add a weather report.
Remove the harmed student.

question.name: CW_U03_L04_R_Q21
question.questiontext: Central idea: Letting go can be an act of care. Which detail supports it?

answer.answertext: The character locks the cage tighter.
The character paints a wall.
The character gives the injured bird space after opening the cage door.
The character ignores the bird's injury.

question.name: CW_U03_L04_R_Q22
question.questiontext: Which explanation is strongest? Central idea: Secrets can damage trust. Detail: The character deletes a message before her friend sees it.

answer.answertext: The deleted message supports the idea because hiding communication creates secrecy between friends.
It supports the idea because it is a sentence.
It supports the idea because phones exist.
It does not matter what details do.

question.name: CW_U03_L04_R_Q23
question.questiontext: Central idea: Persistence means trying again with a wiser plan. Which detail best supports it?

answer.answertext: The character repeats the same mistake without thinking.
The character quits immediately.
The character names the river only.
After the bridge collapses, the character studies the river before rebuilding.

question.name: CW_U03_L04_R_Q24
question.questiontext: What is the best use of central idea during drafting?

answer.answertext: Use it to choose details, conflicts, and character actions that support the same meaning.
Ignore it after writing one sentence.
Use it only for the title.
Replace all details with one vague word.

question.name: CW_U03_L04_R_Q25
question.questiontext: A student writes, "This detail supports the idea because I like it." What feedback is best?

answer.answertext: Personal preference is always enough evidence.
Explain how the detail develops the central idea, not just personal preference.
Remove the central idea from the answer.
Add unrelated details until it feels longer.

question_category.name: CW U3 L5 Reviewed 2026-09-06
question_category.info: The default category for questions shared in context 'U3L5 Q'.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q01
question.questiontext: Passage: The narrator describes a cracked cup each time the family avoids talking about moving. What is the writer's likely purpose?

answer.answertext: To explain how cups are made.
To make the cup a visible sign of family tension.
To remove tension from the scene.
To show that moving is never discussed anywhere.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q02
question.questiontext: Passage: "Naturally, the committee chose the plan that solved nothing and cost twice as much." What rhetorical choice is strongest?

answer.answertext: Neutral description.
Celebration.
Scientific definition.
Sarcasm.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q03
question.questiontext: Passage: The writer delays revealing why the narrator will not enter the house until the last paragraph. What is the likely reader effect?

answer.answertext: It creates suspense and curiosity.
It proves houses are unimportant.
It removes structure.
It makes the ending impossible to understand.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q04
question.questiontext: Passage: "The trophy glittered under the lights, but Mira kept looking at the empty seat in the front row." What craft choice supports purpose?

answer.answertext: A recipe list.
Random weather detail.
Contrast between public success and private absence.
Removing all emotion.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q05
question.questiontext: Passage: A writer wants readers to distrust a narrator. Which choice best supports that purpose?

answer.answertext: The narrator uses paragraphs.
The narrator names a color once.
The narrator describes lunch accurately.
The narrator gives three different versions of the same event.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q06
question.questiontext: Passage: The writer uses a gentle tone when describing a rival's mistake. What purpose might this serve?

answer.answertext: To make the rival seem monstrous.
To invite sympathy instead of ridicule.
To remove reader response.
To explain grammar only.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q07
question.questiontext: Passage: "The hallway narrowed with every step toward the principal's office." What reader effect does the image create?

answer.answertext: It makes anxiety feel physical.
It provides exact architecture measurements.
It creates a happy celebration.
It removes the setting.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q08
question.questiontext: Passage: A writer repeats the phrase "not yet" as a character postpones telling the truth. What is the purpose of repetition?

answer.answertext: To make the scene unrelated.
To prove the character already confessed.
To emphasize delay and avoidance.
To avoid rhetoric.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q09
question.questiontext: Passage: The scene opens with the final argument, then moves backward to show the small choices that caused it. What structural purpose is likely?

answer.answertext: To remove cause and effect.
To make time irrelevant.
To list unrelated events.
To make readers ask how the conflict reached that point.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q10
question.questiontext: Passage: "She smiled so widely that her brother stepped back." What does the detail likely do?

answer.answertext: It hints that the smile may hide anger or pressure.
It proves the scene has no tension.
It explains dentistry.
It removes character response.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q11
question.questiontext: Passage: A writer wants to show grief without naming it. Which craft choice best fits?

answer.answertext: Say "She was sad" five times.
Show the character setting two plates at dinner, then putting one back.
Add unrelated sports scores.
Remove all action.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q12
question.questiontext: Passage: The narrator uses formal, distant language while describing a painful memory. What reader effect might this create?

answer.answertext: It always means the memory is funny.
It removes voice.
It proves the narrator is not affected.
It can show emotional restraint or avoidance.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q13
question.questiontext: Passage: The writer gives the antagonist one quiet moment helping a child. What purpose might this serve?

answer.answertext: To prove the character has no role.
To remove all conflict.
To complicate the reader's view of the character.
To switch genres automatically.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q14
question.questiontext: Passage: "The clock clicked louder each time Ren avoided the question." What craft choice is used?

answer.answertext: Sound detail to increase tension.
A map legend.
A direct definition.
Comic relief only.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q15
question.questiontext: Passage: A writer wants the reader to feel trapped with the character. Which choice best supports this purpose?

answer.answertext: Describe an unrelated picnic.
Use close narration and repeated details of locked exits.
Summarize the scene in one neutral sentence.
Use no setting details.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q16
question.questiontext: Passage: The author includes dialogue where every answer is shorter than the question before it. What effect can this create?

answer.answertext: It always shows joy.
It proves no character is present.
It removes pacing.
It can show a character becoming guarded or unwilling to speak.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q17
question.questiontext: Passage: "The apology sat in my drafts folder all week." What does the object detail do?

answer.answertext: It explains how email servers work.
It proves the apology was spoken.
It makes hesitation visible.
It removes conflict.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q18
question.questiontext: Passage: The writer uses second person: "You keep your hand on the doorknob, pretending you are only checking the lock." What is a likely purpose?

answer.answertext: To place the reader inside the character's anxious self-deception.
To make the scene a recipe.
To reveal every character's thoughts.
To remove setting.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q19
question.questiontext: Passage: A writer wants readers to notice injustice in a school rule. Which rhetorical choice fits?

answer.answertext: Avoid all examples.
Show the rule affecting two students unfairly in the same scene.
Add unrelated weather only.
Make every character agree with the rule.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q20
question.questiontext: Passage: "No one said the word leaving, but every box was labeled in thick black marker." What purpose does the detail serve?

answer.answertext: It proves nobody can read.
It makes moving impossible.
It explains marker chemistry.
It shows the truth of leaving without direct dialogue.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q21
question.questiontext: Passage: Which answer best connects craft choice to purpose?

answer.answertext: The writer slows the moment before the confession so readers feel the character's fear.
The writer has words because stories have words.
The story is long because it is long.
The character exists in the passage.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q22
question.questiontext: Passage: The author describes the town celebration through a character who feels excluded. What purpose might point of view serve?

answer.answertext: It proves celebrations are impossible.
It reveals every townsperson's thoughts.
It makes the celebration feel painful instead of joyful.
It removes tone.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q23
question.questiontext: Passage: A writer cuts a paragraph of explanation and adds one image of a packed suitcase by the door. What purpose might this serve?

answer.answertext: To make the passage less visual.
To show departure through concrete detail instead of telling.
To remove meaning.
To explain suitcase manufacturing.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q24
question.questiontext: Passage: "The mayor called the crumbling bridge 'a minor inconvenience' while drivers turned around one by one." What rhetorical effect is created?

answer.answertext: The bridge disappears.
Everyone agrees there is no problem.
Irony exposes the mayor's understatement.
The sentence has no tone.

question.name: CW_U03_L05_R_Q25
question.questiontext: Passage: A student says, "The author used a detail because details are required." What feedback is best?

answer.answertext: Keep the answer because it is specific enough.
Remove all evidence.
Focus only on punctuation.
Explain what the detail makes readers think, feel, notice, or question.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q01
question.questiontext: Passage: Talia believes asking for feedback proves weakness. By the end, she asks her teacher what to revise first. What coming-of-age change occurs?

answer.answertext: She decides never to revise.
She avoids the teacher forever.
She stops making art.
She learns feedback can be part of growth.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q02
question.questiontext: Passage: Marco thinks his father's traffic rules are control. After his sister nearly rides into traffic, he understands the rules as care. What creates the change?

answer.answertext: The rule disappears.
A new experience reveals the reason behind the rule.
His father admits the rule is useless.
Marco never changes.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q03
question.questiontext: Passage: Lena sees a cracked bowl as clutter, but her mother sees it as memory. What is the conflict?

answer.answertext: A conflict about weather.
A conflict with no object.
Conflicting perspectives about the bowl's meaning.
A conflict about money only.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q04
question.questiontext: Passage: Nia thinks careful register rules are showing off. After nearly giving wrong change, she understands why her brother counts twice. What is her new understanding?

answer.answertext: Careful habits can protect others from mistakes.
Counting is always showing off.
The register is unrelated.
Mistakes do not matter.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q05
question.questiontext: Passage: Eli thinks his grandmother's stories delay chores. After finding her old notebook with the same street names, he asks to hear the story again. What has Eli learned?

answer.answertext: Chores are the only theme.
The stories carry family history.
Street names are random.
He should never listen.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q06
question.questiontext: Which event best shows a coming-of-age turning point?

answer.answertext: A character has a birthday with no change.
A character describes a table.
A character repeats the same belief without challenge.
A character realizes a parent's rule came from care after seeing the danger herself.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q07
question.questiontext: Passage: "I thought the store was just shelves and prices. Then I watched Mom greet every customer by name." What changes?

answer.answertext: The store disappears.
Prices become the only meaning.
The narrator sees the store as community, not just business.
Customers stop mattering.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q08
question.questiontext: Passage: A young narrator insists her older sister is bossy. Later she realizes her sister checked every bus route so they would arrive safely. What is the conflicting perspective?

answer.answertext: The narrator sees control; the sister acts from responsibility.
Both characters agree completely from the start.
The bus route has no role.
The narrator never learns anything.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q09
question.questiontext: Passage: The scene slows as a character reads a message that proves she was wrong about her friend. Why might pacing slow here?

answer.answertext: To skip the realization.
To let the realization feel important.
To remove tension.
To make the message meaningless.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q10
question.questiontext: Passage: "I used to think the garden was punishment. After Grandpa died, I watered the tomatoes before school." What coming-of-age change is shown?

answer.answertext: The narrator hates tomatoes forever.
The garden is unrelated to growth.
The narrator begins to value a responsibility that once felt like punishment.
Grandpa waters the tomatoes.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q11
question.questiontext: Passage: Two characters argue about leaving town. One sees leaving as betrayal; the other sees it as survival. What does this conflict show?

answer.answertext: Both characters think exactly alike.
Leaving has no stakes.
Towns cannot be settings.
Conflicting perspectives can make the same choice mean different things.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q12
question.questiontext: Passage: A narrator says, "I knew Dad was being dramatic," but later admits, "I had mistaken worry for weakness." What changes?

answer.answertext: Dad disappears from the story.
The narrator's perspective on Dad's emotion matures.
Worry is proven useless.
The narrator never admits anything.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q13
question.questiontext: Which statement best defines coming of age?

answer.answertext: A character grows in understanding because of experience, conflict, or realization.
A character only gets older.
A story has no conflict.
A character never changes.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q14
question.questiontext: Passage: "The argument with my aunt sounded smaller after I read the letter she wrote at my age." What causes the narrator's shift?

answer.answertext: Forgetting the argument completely.
Ignoring the letter.
Seeing the aunt's younger perspective through the letter.
Hearing no new information.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q15
question.questiontext: Passage: A character thinks courage means never being afraid. Later she speaks at the meeting while her hands shake. What realization is shown?

answer.answertext: Courage means silence.
Fear prevents all action.
Meetings cannot matter.
Courage can happen while fear is present.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q16
question.questiontext: Passage: "Mom called it tradition. I called it a waste of Saturdays. Then the neighbors came for the soup before the storm." What perspective changes?

answer.answertext: Mom stops caring about tradition.
The narrator sees the tradition as community care.
Soup becomes unrelated.
Saturdays disappear.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q17
question.questiontext: Which evidence best proves a character's perspective has changed?

answer.answertext: The character acts differently after a realization.
The character's name is mentioned twice.
The setting has a wall.
The passage has punctuation.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q18
question.questiontext: Passage: "I thought my cousin was showing off when she translated for Grandma. Later, I realized she was making sure Grandma could answer for herself." What is the new understanding?

answer.answertext: Translation is always showing off.
Grandma has no role.
Translation can give someone voice rather than take attention.
The cousin stops translating.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q19
question.questiontext: Passage: A scene uses close first-person narration during a realization. What effect can this create?

answer.answertext: Readers know every character's thoughts equally.
The realization becomes impossible.
The passage loses perspective.
Readers experience the character's changing thoughts directly.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q20
question.questiontext: Passage: The narrator argues that rules are pointless. After a younger child gets hurt ignoring them, the narrator changes. Which theme is strongest?

answer.answertext: Rules never matter.
Maturity can mean understanding the purpose behind limits.
Younger children cannot affect stories.
Arguments always solve everything.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q21
question.questiontext: Passage: "At first, June called the old photos clutter. By the end, she labeled each one before packing them." What does this show?

answer.answertext: June throws the photos away.
June never changes.
June's perspective on memory changes.
Photos are not part of the passage.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q22
question.questiontext: What is a blind spot in coming-of-age fiction?

answer.answertext: Something a character does not yet understand.
A literal eye injury in every story.
A setting with no light only.
A detail that always stays hidden.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q23
question.questiontext: Passage: The narrator resents helping at the food pantry until she recognizes her classmate in line. What changes?

answer.answertext: The pantry disappears.
Helping is proven useless.
The classmate has no role.
The narrator sees the work as connected to real people, not an abstract chore.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q24
question.questiontext: Passage: A character and parent disagree: the character wants freedom; the parent worries about safety. What makes this a useful conflict?

answer.answertext: Both perspectives have understandable reasons.
Only one character can have a reason.
Safety and freedom cannot conflict.
Parent characters cannot matter.

question.name: CW_U03_L06_R_Q25
question.questiontext: A student writes, "The character comes of age because she is sixteen." What feedback is best?

answer.answertext: Keep the answer because all ages prove growth.
Explain how her understanding changes; age alone is not enough.
Remove all evidence.
Focus only on the birthday date.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q01
question.questiontext: Scene plan: Theme: belonging requires invitation. Conflict: a student is excluded from a lunch table. Detail: one character moves a backpack to make room. What makes the plan integrated?

answer.answertext: The backpack is unrelated to the scene.
The conflict and detail both support belonging.
The theme should be removed.
Exclusion prevents all fiction development.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q02
question.questiontext: Passage: Imani thinks winning means standing alone. Her mentor gives her a list of names before the final project and says, "No one builds a bridge by holding one rope." What source pattern is most likely adapted?

answer.answertext: A random recipe.
A conflict with no source influence.
A copied original plot.
A guide gives an object before a difficult journey.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q03
question.questiontext: Central idea: responsibility is shared. Which character change best supports it?

answer.answertext: The character moves from controlling every task to trusting teammates with important work.
The character refuses all help forever.
The character changes shoes.
The character forgets the project.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q04
question.questiontext: A scene adapts a warning-before-risk pattern. The character ignores a lab partner's warning and launches the project early. What theme can this support?

answer.answertext: Warnings have no purpose.
Labs cannot be adapted settings.
Pride can make a person ignore useful guidance.
Risk always leads to success.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q05
question.questiontext: Which plan best integrates author purpose with central idea?

answer.answertext: Purpose: show kindness; central idea: weather is cold; detail: a random clock.
Purpose: create humor; central idea: honesty matters; detail: unrelated shoes.
Purpose: no reader effect; central idea: none; detail: everything.
Purpose: make readers question independence; central idea: accepting help can show maturity; detail: character finally hands a box to a friend.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q06
question.questiontext: Passage: A character keeps an old recipe card while moving to a new city and later cooks from it for a lonely neighbor. Which skills are integrated?

answer.answertext: Only punctuation.
Theme, meaningful object, and character action.
A source with no transformation.
No central idea.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q07
question.questiontext: A student's fiction plan includes a source object that never appears after the first sentence. What is the best revision?

answer.answertext: Make the object affect the conflict or character change.
Add five more unused objects.
Remove the character growth.
Keep it because all objects are automatically symbolic.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q08
question.questiontext: Scene plan: Starting belief: asking for help means failure. Conflicting perspective: a coach says revision is part of excellence. Changed understanding: the character asks for critique. What kind of arc is this?

answer.answertext: A setting list only.
A theme with no character.
Coming-of-age growth arc.
A copied source.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q09
question.questiontext: Which detail best supports a theme about honesty repairing harm?

answer.answertext: The character changes socks.
The character ignores the person harmed.
The character describes the ceiling only.
The character returns the hidden letter and apologizes directly.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q10
question.questiontext: Passage: A narrator thinks family stories waste time until an old notebook proves the streets in the stories were real. What reader effect does the notebook create?

answer.answertext: It makes the narrator's changed understanding believable.
It removes family history.
It makes the stories pointless.
It creates no effect.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q11
question.questiontext: What is the strongest integrated fiction planning sequence?

answer.answertext: Random object, random setting, random dialogue, no purpose.
Central idea, character belief, conflict, source/detail choices, changed understanding.
Ending first, then remove all evidence.
Theme only with no scene.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q12
question.questiontext: Passage: The map from a teammate appears when the leader gets lost and finally asks the team to choose the route together. What does the map do?

answer.answertext: It distracts because maps can never matter.
It proves the leader should work alone.
It removes the team.
It supports the theme that leadership can require shared guidance.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q13
question.questiontext: A plan compares two themes: one passage shows courage through speaking up; another shows courage through leaving an unsafe place. What should the comparison explain?

answer.answertext: Only that both have characters.
That the passages are identical.
How both develop courage differently through different actions.
That courage has no evidence.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q14
question.questiontext: Which source influence best supports a character learning humility?

answer.answertext: A pride-before-fall pattern transformed into a student ignoring advice before a performance.
A random lunch with no conflict.
A copied ending with no change.
A weather report only.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q15
question.questiontext: Passage: The narrator repeats "I had it under control" before each mistake. What purpose does the repetition serve?

answer.answertext: It proves control is perfect.
It reveals the narrator's blind spot about control.
It removes character perspective.
It explains grammar.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q16
question.questiontext: Central idea: memory can guide a person forward. Which adapted object fits best?

answer.answertext: An unrelated parking ticket.
A random pencil with no role.
A copied magical object with no transformation.
A grandmother's recipe card used in a new city.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q17
question.questiontext: A student's scene has theme, conflict, and growth, but no evidence in the explanation. What should be added?

answer.answertext: More vague praise.
A completely unrelated summary.
Specific passage details showing how the elements develop the idea.
No details at all.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q18
question.questiontext: Passage: The old key no longer opens the house, but the character keeps it while choosing a new apartment. What central idea might it support?

answer.answertext: Leaving can include carrying memory forward.
Keys are useless in every story.
Apartments cannot have themes.
Memory prevents all change.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q19
question.questiontext: Which plan best shows conflicting perspectives?

answer.answertext: Both characters agree without tension.
One character sees moving as betrayal, while another sees it as survival.
A character names every object in a room.
No character has an opinion.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q20
question.questiontext: What makes an adaptation purposeful in integrated fiction?

answer.answertext: It changes only font.
It copies everything.
It has no reason.
The transformed source element affects theme, conflict, or character growth.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q21
question.questiontext: Scene plan: A character wants independence, receives a mentor's marked-up draft, resists feedback, then revises successfully. What theme is strongest?

answer.answertext: Growth can require accepting guidance.
Feedback always ruins writing.
Independence means ignoring everyone.
Drafts have no meaning.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q22
question.questiontext: Which response best explains integration?

answer.answertext: The story uses many names.
The writer avoids revision.
The source object, central idea, and character change all point to the same reader effect.
The setting is long.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q23
question.questiontext: Passage: A character says courage means never fearing anything, then speaks while her hands shake. What changed understanding appears?

answer.answertext: Courage means silence.
Courage can exist while fear is still present.
Fear stops all action.
Hands are the theme.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q24
question.questiontext: A scene has a strong central idea but an unrelated comic side plot that takes half the scene. What revision is best?

answer.answertext: Add more unrelated comedy.
Remove the central idea.
Cut or revise the side plot so it supports the central idea.
Keep everything because length equals quality.

question.name: CW_U03_L07_R_Q25
question.questiontext: Which final check best prepares an integrated fiction scene?

answer.answertext: Did I add details randomly?
Did I remove all character change?
Did I ignore evidence?
Do theme, source influence, central idea, purpose, conflict, and growth support the same effect?

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q01
question.questiontext: Passage: A character gives up a winning speech slot to help a nervous friend prepare. What universal theme is best supported?

answer.answertext: Speeches are always short.

Winning never matters.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q02
question.questiontext: Source element: A guide gives an object before a journey. Adaptation: A coach gives a route card before a city race. What is preserved?

answer.answertext: The exact original setting.

No source connection.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q03
question.questiontext: Central idea: Avoiding responsibility can make guilt grow. Which detail best supports it?

answer.answertext: The wall is painted white.
A dog walks outside.

The character eats breakfast.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q04
question.questiontext: Passage: "Naturally, the committee solved the leak by buying a larger bucket." What rhetorical choice is strongest?

answer.answertext: Sarcasm criticizing an ineffective solution.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q05
question.questiontext: Passage: Eli thinks family stories delay chores until he finds the same street names in his grandmother's old notebook. What changes?

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q06
question.questiontext: Passage A: Lina practices alone after failure. Passage B: Theo asks for help after failure. What comparison is strongest?

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q07
question.questiontext: Passage: Talia thinks asking for critique proves weakness, but later asks what to revise first. What coming-of-age change is shown?

answer.answertext: She refuses all revision.
She stops making art.
She learns feedback can be part of growth.
She avoids the teacher.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q08
question.questiontext: What is a complete theme statement?

answer.answertext: Friendship can require honesty even when honesty is uncomfortable.
Friendship.
The story has a friend.
Blue jacket.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q09
question.questiontext: A student adapts a source by changing only character names while keeping the exact plot and ending. What is the problem?

answer.answertext: It changes too much.
It is too close to copying and lacks meaningful transformation.
It has no source connection.
It is automatically respectful.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q10
question.questiontext: Passage: The clock ticks louder each time Ren avoids the question. What is the reader effect?

answer.answertext: The clock explains math.
The question disappears.
The sound detail increases tension around avoidance.
The scene becomes cheerful.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q11
question.questiontext: Central idea: Memory can make a new place feel less lonely. Which revision best supports it?

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q12
question.questiontext: Passage: A narrator repeats "not yet" while postponing the truth. What author purpose is likely?

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q13
question.questiontext: Which detail best supports "courage can exist beside fear"?

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q14
question.questiontext: Source element: A forbidden door tests curiosity. Adaptation: A student is warned not to open a locked digital folder. What is preserved?

The same time period.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q15
question.questiontext: Passage: A character returns a trophy after learning the score was wrong. What theme is strongest?

Doing what is right can matter more than public praise.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q16
question.questiontext: Which explanation best connects evidence to central idea? Central idea: Secrets damage trust. Detail: The character deletes a message before a friend sees it.

Details do not need connection.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q17
question.questiontext: Passage: "Of course the award went to the student who arrived late and bowed like royalty." What tone is created?

answer.answertext: Sarcastic and critical.
Completely neutral.
Scientific.
Grateful.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q18
question.questiontext: What should a rationale for adaptation include?

answer.answertext: Only a new name.
No explanation.
Source element, transformation, and reason for the change.
Only punctuation.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q19
question.questiontext: Passage: A character thinks leadership means doing everything alone, then succeeds only after trusting the team. What central idea is best supported?

answer.answertext: Teams always fail.
Leaders should never trust anyone.
Responsibility is unrelated.
Leadership can require shared responsibility.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q20
question.questiontext: Passage: A narrator leaves home but packs a recipe card first. What theme is best supported?

answer.answertext: Recipes erase memory.
Change can include carrying meaningful parts of the past forward.
Moving means forgetting everything.
Home is never important.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q21
question.questiontext: What is a blind spot in coming-of-age fiction?

answer.answertext: A required eye injury.
A random setting detail.
Something a character does not yet understand.
A complete theme statement.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q22
question.questiontext: Passage: The writer gives the antagonist a quiet moment helping a child. What purpose might this serve?

answer.answertext: To remove all conflict.
To prove the character has no role.
To change the passage into a recipe.
To complicate the reader's view of the character.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q23
question.questiontext: Which comparison is strongest? Passage A: a child returns a stolen coin. Passage B: a merchant corrects an overpayment.

answer.answertext: Both develop integrity through returning what does not belong to the character.
Coins and merchants are identical.
Only children can be honest.
Money removes theme.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q24
question.questiontext: Scene plan: central idea about belonging, conflict about exclusion, and detail of a shared table. What makes it integrated?

answer.answertext: It uses unrelated details.
The conflict and table detail both support the belonging idea.
The table has no role.
The central idea should be removed.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q25
question.questiontext: A student writes, "The theme is that Kai finds a coin." What feedback is best?

answer.answertext: Revise because that is a plot detail; explain the larger idea the coin supports.
Keep it because all plot details are themes.
Remove all evidence.
Use one word only.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q26
question.questiontext: Passage: Lena wanted to ignore the new student because everyone else did. At lunch, she moved her tray to the empty seat beside him. Which theme statement is strongest?

answer.answertext: Lunch can happen at school.
The topic is students.
Lena has a tray.
Belonging often begins when one person chooses kindness over comfort.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q27
question.questiontext: Passage: Tomas wanted to win the art prize, but he helped his tired partner finish her mural before starting his own final details. What topic and theme are best supported?

answer.answertext: Topic: paint; Theme: Paint is colorful.
Topic: sleep; Theme: Everyone should nap.
Topic: ambition and teamwork; Theme: Personal goals can still leave room for helping others.
Topic: prizes; Theme: Prizes always ruin friendships.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q28
question.questiontext: Passage: Asha kept the cracked bracelet after her friend moved away. She wore it on the first day at a new school, touching it before she introduced herself. What does the bracelet help develop?

answer.answertext: A theme about jewelry prices.
A theme about memory giving strength during change.
A rule that all bracelets are cracked.
A summary that Asha has a bracelet.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q29
question.questiontext: Passage A: Rina gave her last pencil to a classmate before the exam. Passage B: Omar shared his umbrella even though his own sleeve got soaked. What shared theme is best supported?

answer.answertext: School supplies and umbrellas are the same object.
Weather is always more important than school.
Exams should happen in the rain.
Helping others can require giving up personal comfort or convenience.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q30
question.questiontext: Passage A: Mina apologized after blaming her brother for the spill. Passage B: Carter returned the borrowed book after pretending he had lost it. How are the themes similar?

answer.answertext: Both show that honesty can repair damage after a mistake.
Both are mainly about cleaning.
Both show that books are dangerous.
Both prove apologies are useless.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q31
question.questiontext: Source element: A character receives a warning before making a risky choice. Adaptation: A student ignores a teammate's warning about faulty robot code before the final round. What is preserved?

answer.answertext: The exact original setting.
The character names from the source.
The warning before a risky choice.
The complete original plot.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q32
question.questiontext: Source element: A guide gives a traveler a protective object. Adaptation: A grandmother gives a narrator a recipe card before the narrator moves to a new city. What is transformed?

answer.answertext: The source is copied exactly.
The protective object becomes emotional support through a recipe card.
The adaptation removes all source connection.
The character has no journey.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q33
question.questiontext: Central idea: Avoiding responsibility can make guilt grow. Passage detail: Niko hides the baseball under three blankets after blaming the broken window on the wind. How does the detail support the central idea?

answer.answertext: It shows Niko likes blankets.
It proves the wind broke the window.
It distracts from the central idea completely.
It shows Niko's guilt growing through secretive action.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q34
question.questiontext: Central idea: Accepting help can be a form of strength. Which detail best supports the idea?

answer.answertext: The character describes an unrelated poster for three paragraphs.
The character refuses all help and leaves.
The character hands one heavy box to a friend and keeps walking beside her.
The character counts clouds.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q35
question.questiontext: Passage: The writer repeats the image of an empty chair at dinner before explaining who is missing. What is the most likely purpose?

answer.answertext: To make the reader feel absence before receiving full explanation.
To describe furniture only.
To prove the chair is new.
To avoid all emotion.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q36
question.questiontext: Passage: "Of course the award went to the student who forgot the speech and bowed like royalty." What craft choice is strongest?

answer.answertext: Warm admiration.
Sarcastic tone.
Neutral listing.
Scientific explanation.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q37
question.questiontext: Passage: Talia thinks asking for critique proves she is not ready for advanced art. After her teacher explains that artists revise through feedback, Talia asks what to change first. What is Talia's changed understanding?

answer.answertext: Artists never revise.
Asking questions proves failure.
Feedback can be part of serious growth.
Advanced art has no challenge.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q38
question.questiontext: Passage: Marco thinks his father's traffic rules are about control. After his sister almost rides into the street, he understands why his father checks twice. What causes Marco's change?

answer.answertext: He forgets the rule.
His father disappears.
The street becomes irrelevant.
He sees the safety reason behind the rule.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q39
question.questiontext: Scene plan: Central idea: maturity includes accepting guidance. Source influence: a guide gives an object before a journey. Character conflict: Maya thinks leaders work alone, while her teammate thinks leaders trust the group. Which choice best explains integration?

answer.answertext: The plan is integrated because every element supports shared responsibility.
The plan is integrated because it has many unrelated parts.
The source influence distracts because objects can never develop theme.
The conflict should be removed so the theme is easier.

question.name: CW_U03_UA_R_Q40
question.questiontext: Passage: Jalen believed the mural had to be his design alone. When Amara handed him a sketch showing how everyone's ideas could fit, he erased his signature from the center and redrew the wall as a shared map. What changed understanding is shown?

answer.answertext: Jalen learns maps are never useful.
Jalen learns that leadership can include shared creative ownership.
Jalen decides art has no theme.
Jalen avoids all collaboration.

Define a poetry term generally without applying it to the line.

question.name: CW_U04_PRE_R_Q03

Define a poetry term generally without applying it to the line.

Define a poetry term generally without applying it to the line.
Choose based on length or surface topic instead of craft effect.

question.name: CW_U04_PRE_R_Q05
question.questiontext: Unit 4 pretest item. Poem/context: The hallway swallowed my footsteps. What is the strongest response?

question.name: CW_U04_PRE_R_Q06
question.questiontext: Unit 4 pretest item. Poem/context: The word slender appears instead of scrawny. What is the strongest response?

Answer from personal opinion without textual evidence.
Define a poetry term generally without applying it to the line.
Choose based on length or surface topic instead of craft effect.

question.name: CW_U04_PRE_R_Q07
question.questiontext: Unit 4 pretest item. Poem/context: The last bus sighed away. What is the strongest response?

answer.answertext: Answer from personal opinion without textual evidence.
The verb sighed personifies the bus and creates a weary mood of departure and finality.
Define a poetry term generally without applying it to the line.
Choose based on length or surface topic instead of craft effect.

question.name: CW_U04_PRE_R_Q08
question.questiontext: Unit 4 pretest item. Poem/context: The bridge disappeared in fog. What is the strongest response?

answer.answertext: Answer from personal opinion without textual evidence.
Define a poetry term generally without applying it to the line.
Choose based on length or surface topic instead of craft effect.
The disappearing bridge creates uncertainty because the path ahead is hidden by fog.

question.name: CW_U04_PRE_R_Q09
question.questiontext: Unit 4 pretest item. Poem/context: The candle made an island of light. What is the strongest response?

answer.answertext: The metaphor compares candlelight to an island, emphasizing a small refuge within darkness.
Answer from personal opinion without textual evidence.
Define a poetry term generally without applying it to the line.
Choose based on length or surface topic instead of craft effect.

question.name: CW_U04_PRE_R_Q10
question.questiontext: Unit 4 pretest item. Poem/context: The speaker says the city hummed under the rain. What is the strongest response?

answer.answertext: Answer from personal opinion without textual evidence.
Define a poetry term generally without applying it to the line.
Personification makes the city seem steadily alive, creating a subdued but active mood.
Choose based on length or surface topic instead of craft effect.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q01
question.questiontext: Which action best begins integrated portfolio preparation?

answer.answertext: List required parts and mark each present, missing, or needing revision.
Decorate the portfolio before checking contents.
Submit the first file found.
Remove the author statement.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q02
question.questiontext: Which piece belongs in a final portfolio?

answer.answertext: A piece with no title and no revision.
A favorite piece the writer cannot explain.
A revised piece that shows a specific craft skill and reader effect.
A draft with comments still visible.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q03
question.questiontext: A portfolio statement discusses voice. Which evidence best matches it?

answer.answertext: A random image pasted beside the title.
A file name with no writing attached.
A paragraph saying the writer worked hard.
A revised story excerpt where dialogue and sentence rhythm reveal character voice.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q04
question.questiontext: Which portfolio order has the clearest purpose?

answer.answertext: Alphabetical by file name with no explanation.
Story first for revised dialogue, poem second for voice through rhythm, statement last to explain growth.
Random order based on download time.
Longest to shortest only because length matters most.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q05
question.questiontext: Which note is most useful during a readiness pass?

answer.answertext: Fix it later.
Maybe change something.
Preview script and make character labels consistent.
It looks fine from far away.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q06
question.questiontext: How should an author statement connect to selected pieces?

answer.answertext: It should name skills the reader can see in the portfolio.
It should discuss unrelated goals only.
It should hide all revision evidence.
It should replace the creative pieces.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q07
question.questiontext: Which presentation choice best supports the portfolio?

answer.answertext: Read the longest excerpt regardless of purpose.
Avoid explaining the excerpt.
Summarize every assignment from the course.
Choose one excerpt that shows a craft choice connected to portfolio growth.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q08
question.questiontext: Which problem should be fixed before final publication?

answer.answertext: The writer can explain the piece clearly.
The final file includes bracketed notes that say add ending later.
The portfolio has a clear title.
The author statement names revision growth.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q09
question.questiontext: What makes a portfolio integrated?

answer.answertext: The files are unrelated but colorful.
The portfolio has no explanation.
The selected pieces, statement, revision evidence, and presentation plan connect to shared growth.
The presentation ignores the pieces.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q10
question.questiontext: Which answer best explains reader effect?

answer.answertext: I put this first because I found it first.
I added random spacing.
I like the color.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q11
question.questiontext: A student marks "needs revision" beside the presentation plan. What should come next?

answer.answertext: Write the exact missing action, such as add listening focus.
Ignore the note.
Delete the portfolio.
Submit without checking.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q12
question.questiontext: Which choice shows revision evidence?

answer.answertext: A blank page.
A final piece with no explanation and no draft trail.
A draft and final version with a note explaining how feedback improved dialogue.
A decoration folder.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q13
question.questiontext: Which author rationale is strongest?

answer.answertext: I included this because it was easy.
I included this poem because revising the image pattern made the speaker's change clearer.
I included this because it is first alphabetically.
I included this because I needed another page.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q14
question.questiontext: Which statement describes publication formatting?

answer.answertext: Changing the genre completely.
Avoiding all revision.
Refusing to preview the file.
Preparing the piece with title, spacing, labels, conventions, and file readiness.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q15
question.questiontext: What should a student do if the portfolio order feels random?

answer.answertext: Create a reader-focused order and explain the reason.
Leave it random.
Remove every piece.
Add unrelated colors.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q16
question.questiontext: Which checkpoint response shows mastery?

answer.answertext: I am done because I clicked submit.
I chose whatever was easiest.
My portfolio order moves from revised story to poem to statement so readers see voice growth across genres.
I cannot explain the order.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q17
question.questiontext: Which final presentation note is strongest?

answer.answertext: Listen to everything.
Listen for how the clipped dialogue creates tension after the narrator avoids the question.
I do not know what to listen for.
Ignore the excerpt.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q18
question.questiontext: Which issue is a portfolio completeness problem?

answer.answertext: The title is clear.
The presentation has a listening focus.
The revised piece has paragraph breaks.
The required author statement is missing.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q19
question.questiontext: Why should the student avoid vague notes like "fix portfolio"?

answer.answertext: They do not identify the exact action needed.
They are too detailed.
They replace the need for revision.
They prove mastery.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q20
question.questiontext: Which answer best connects publication and presentation?

answer.answertext: The presentation should ignore the portfolio.
Publication means no one reads the piece.
The portfolio shows the final work, and the presentation explains how selected craft choices work.
Presentation means only summary.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q21
question.questiontext: Which choice should be removed from a final portfolio file?

answer.answertext: Clear title.
Intentional line breaks.
Author name if required.
Unresolved comment saying check spelling.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q22
question.questiontext: Which answer is strongest when explaining a selected excerpt?

I selected it because it shows the exact revision I describe in my statement.

I selected it but will not explain it.

question.name: CW_U06_L07_R_Q23
question.questiontext: Which readiness pass checks genre-specific format?

answer.answertext: Check poems for intentional line breaks and scripts for clear character labels.
Make every genre look identical.
Remove all titles.
Add random spacing.

Delete all reflection.
Ignore the mismatch.

answer.answertext: Submit one rough draft only.
Submit a presentation with no portfolio.

question.name: CW_U06_UA_R_Q32
question.questiontext: Story problem: A suspense scene moves too quickly. Which revision best improves pacing?

answer.answertext: Add action beats as the character listens at the door and watches the light shift.
Remove the entire scene.
Add a random joke.
Change every name.

question.name: CW_U06_UA_R_Q33
question.questiontext: Poem problem: The line says, "I felt sad." Feedback asks for a stronger image. Which revision best fits?

answer.answertext: I felt very sad and sadder.
Sadness is a feeling.
Rain gathered on the sill until the glass forgot the street.
I deleted the poem.

question.name: CW_U06_UA_R_Q34
question.questiontext: Poem problem: The final choice happens too quickly. Which revision best uses line breaks?

answer.answertext: Add random breaks after every letter.
Place the final phrase on its own line so the reader pauses before the decision.
Remove all line breaks forever.
Change the poem into a grocery list.

question.name: CW_U06_UA_R_Q35
question.questiontext: A student is preparing a poem for digital publication. Which formatting choice best supports the genre?

answer.answertext: Put the entire poem in one paragraph so it uses less space.
Add random symbols before every line.
Remove the title because poems do not need one.
Keep the title clear and preserve purposeful line and stanza breaks.

question.name: CW_U06_UA_R_Q36
question.questiontext: A short story draft appears as one long block of text with dialogue inside the same paragraph. What should the writer do first?

answer.answertext: Add paragraph breaks when the speaker changes and when the action shifts.
Change every sentence to a different font.
Remove all dialogue marks.
Add extra blank lines after every sentence.

question.name: CW_U06_UA_R_Q37
question.questiontext: An author presentation begins with a short story excerpt. Which opening best prepares the audience?

answer.answertext: I am reading something I wrote, and that is all you need to know.
My piece is a short story called The Last Bus. Listen for the short sentences because they show panic.
This is long, so I will explain every event before reading.
I picked this because it is my favorite.

question.name: CW_U06_UA_R_Q38
question.questiontext: Which excerpt choice is strongest for an author presentation?

answer.answertext: The longest section, even if it needs ten minutes of explanation.
A random middle section with no context.
A short section that clearly shows a craft choice and can be understood with brief context.
The first page only because first pages are always best.

question.name: CW_U06_UA_R_Q39
question.questiontext: Which portfolio choice is strongest?

answer.answertext: Choose the longest piece only because it fills space.
Choose the favorite piece with no explanation.
Choose a piece with unresolved draft comments.
Choose a revised piece that shows clear craft growth and can be explained.

question.name: CW_U06_UA_R_Q40
question.questiontext: A student notices the author statement discusses imagery, but no selected piece shows imagery. What should the student do?

answer.answertext: Revise the statement or portfolio so the evidence and explanation match.
Leave the mismatch because readers will guess.
Remove all craft language from the statement.
Add random images to every page.
